newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain up in arms over proposed EU olive oil reform.
newsitem.headline: Spain up in arms over proposed EU olive oil reform.

text.p: Spain criticised the European Commission's proposal for sweeping reforms of the olive oil industry on Wednesday and will seek support of other countries to block the plan.
Spain's strong opposition to the Commission's efforts was highlighted this week during a visit by EU Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler, who met officials and producers to discuss the changes.
The Commission proposes to reform subsidies that provide a lifeline to EU producers. The EU hopes the changes will distribute aid more fairly and stamp out widespread fraud.

But Spanish officials complain that the reforms, which would change the basis on which aid is allocated, would cost tens of thousands of jobs and hurt production in Spain, Europe's biggest olive oil supplier.

"We must maintain the unity between the five producing countries to block the reform ... and we must also convince other EU colleagues," Spain's Agriculture Minister Loyola de Palacio told state radio.

Calling the industry vital to the survival of some parts of the country, she said: "Those who understand olive production will reject the Commission's key proposal, which would have negative results for production, quality and jobs."
Pressure for reform has grown as the EU faces a burgeoning olive oil surplus. Subsidised exports of 120,000 tonnes a year are already running over the level allowed under the world farm trade pact.
The EU is also struggling to control subsidy fraud, which according to official estimates is 10 times greater than for cereals and other crops in southern EU countries.
The Commission is due to draft a proposal for approval by EU farm ministers after it has received reactions to its proposed reforms from the olive oil industry and the European Parliament.
Spain's National Olive Council said it was ready to take measures to protest the reforms. "We must start to turn the heat up and adopt drastic measures," spokesman Antonio Luque said.
The EU spent 1.8 billion Ecus ($2.1 billion) last year in subsidising the EU's two million olive oil farmers in Italy, Greece, Spain, Portugal and France.
Fischler presented a controversial report in February suggesting two key options for reform.
The first option, favoured by the Commission, would link aid to the number of olive trees and historical regional yields rather than the current system of linking aid to production.

The second option, favoured by most producers, would retain the current system, with aid based on production and consumption, but it would be simplified by having a single system for small and large producers.
But de Palacio complained the Commission had effectively brushed aside the second option.

"Fischler has presented two options and we have been given time to discuss both these options, not just the option based on trees that the Commissioner is pushing," de Palacio said. --Madrid newsroom + 34 1 585 2161
